Waves

What you will learn

  • A wave is a self-propagating disturbance that carries energy, momentum, and information through a medium without transporting matter. We describe it by a function of position and time, u(x,t)u(x,t)u(x,t).

  • Any shape that moves without changing form is a function of x∓vtx \mp vtx∓vt. The periodic case is the sine wave Asin⁡(kx−ωt)A\sin(kx-\omega t)Asin(kx−ωt), and its complex form Aei(kx−ωt)Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)}Aei(kx−ωt) turns the algebra of waves into multiplication.

  • Two periodicities: the wavelength λ\lambdaλ in space and the period TTT in time, packaged as k=2π/λk=2\pi/\lambdak=2π/λ and ω=2π/T\omega=2\pi/Tω=2π/T and tied together by the speed, v=ω/k=λνv=\omega/k=\lambda\nuv=ω/k=λν.

  • Every wave f(x∓vt)f(x \mp vt)f(x∓vt) obeys the same equation, the classical wave equation uxx=utt/v2u_{xx}=u_{tt}/v^2uxx​=utt​/v2.

  • Waves add. Because the wave equation is linear, interference, standing waves, and beats are all superpositions of simpler waves.

  • Light is the one wave without a medium. Its speed is the same for every observer, and that single fact forces moving clocks to run slow.

Types of waves¶

  • Disturbance of a medium: sound waves, waves on a guitar string, ripples on the surface of water.

  • Quantum mechanical waves: described by complex wavefunctions, which explain the wave-like behavior of electrons and atoms.

  • Electromagnetic waves (light, UV, X-rays): the only kind of wave that needs no medium. EM waves travel in vacuum; in a sense an EM wave “rolls out its own carpet,” creating its own medium as it moves forward.

  • Gravitational waves traveling through spacetime.

Waves also differ in which way the medium moves. In a transverse wave the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of travel (a string, light). In a longitudinal wave the disturbance is along the direction of travel (sound in air, a compressed spring). In both cases the beads of the medium only oscillate about their resting positions; only the pattern travels.

# synced: transverse_longitudinal
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
N, A, k, w = 48, 0.35, 2 * np.pi / 4.0, 2 * np.pi / 2.0   # beads, amplitude, lambda = 4, T = 2
x0 = np.linspace(0, 12, N)
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 600)
ts = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi / w, 40, endpoint=False)
pick = 18                                                 # the bead we follow

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 4.6))
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 12.5); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.45)
    ax.set_yticks([]); ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(12.3, 1.1), xytext=(10.3, 1.1), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GRAY, lw=1.6))
    ax.text(11.3, 1.22, "wave moves", color=GRAY, fontsize=10, ha="center")
    ax.axvline(x0[pick], color=CARDINAL, lw=1, ls=":")
ax1.set_title("transverse: each bead moves up and down, perpendicular to the wave", loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
ax2.set_title("longitudinal: each bead moves back and forth, along the wave", loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
ax2.set_xlabel("x")
(string,) = ax1.plot([], [], color=TEAL, lw=1.2, alpha=0.6)
(beads1,) = ax1.plot([], [], "o", color=TEAL, ms=5)
(red1,) = ax1.plot([], [], "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=9, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
(beads2,) = ax2.plot([], [], "o", color=TEAL, ms=6)
(red2,) = ax2.plot([], [], "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=9, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
fig.tight_layout()

def update(i):
    t = ts[i]
    string.set_data(xs, 0.8 * np.sin(k * xs - w * t))
    beads1.set_data(x0, 0.8 * np.sin(k * x0 - w * t))
    red1.set_data([x0[pick]], [0.8 * np.sin(k * x0[pick] - w * t)])
    xl = x0 + A * np.sin(k * x0 - w * t)
    beads2.set_data(xl, np.zeros(N))
    red2.set_data([xl[pick]], [0])

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=75, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)

Defining a wave mathematically¶

  • Since a wave is a moving disturbance uuu, we describe this disturbance (e.g. the vertical displacement of a string) as a function of space xxx and time ttt:

u=f(x,t)u = f(x, t)u=f(x,t)
(1)

  • Imagine surfing on an ocean wave. For an observer riding the wave, the wave stays still at the same coordinate x′x'x′.

  • For an observer standing on the shore, the coordinate xxx of the wave front moves away with a constant velocity:

x=x′+vtx=x'+vtx=x′+vt
(2)

  • Assuming that the shape of the wave stays the same, the shore observer sees the surfer’s frozen shape f(x′)f(x')f(x′) carried along:

u(x,t)=f(x′)=f(x−vt)u(x,t) = f(x')=f(x-vt)u(x,t)=f(x′)=f(x−vt)
(3)

  • To see why f(x−vt)f(x-vt)f(x−vt) moves to the right, follow one point of the shape, say its peak, by holding the argument fixed: x−vt=constx-vt=\text{const}x−vt=const gives x=vt+constx = vt +\text{const}x=vt+const, a point moving right at speed vvv. The same reasoning shows that f(x+vt)f(x+vt)f(x+vt) moves to the left.

from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

(left,) = ax.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=2.2, ls="--", label=r"$f(x+vt)$  moves left")

Periodic traveling waves¶

  • We will work a lot with periodic waves, whose repeating shape can be described by a sine, a cosine, or a combination of the two. The general sine profile is

y(x)=Asin⁡(kx+ϕ)y(x)= A \sin(kx+\phi)y(x)=Asin(kx+ϕ)
(4)

  • To set it in motion, replace xxx by x−vtx - vtx−vt:

y(x,t)=Asin⁡(k(x−vt)+ϕ)=Asin⁡(kx−ωt+ϕ)y(x,t)= A \sin\big(k(x-vt)+\phi\big)=A \sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)y(x,t)=Asin(k(x−vt)+ϕ)=Asin(kx−ωt+ϕ)
(5)

  • Amplitude AAA: the maximum disturbance.

  • Wave number kkk: how fast the phase advances in space.

  • Angular frequency ω=kv\omega=kvω=kv: how fast the phase advances in time.

  • Initial phase ϕ\phiϕ: where the wave starts at t=0t=0t=0, x=0x=0x=0. Often we just set ϕ=0\phi=0ϕ=0.

A periodic traveling wave repeats in two directions: along xxx at a fixed instant (a photograph of the wave) and along ttt at a fixed place (the history of one bead). The animation shows both views at once.

# synced: wavelength_period
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
lam, T = 4.0, 2.0
k, w = 2 * np.pi / lam, 2 * np.pi / T
x = np.linspace(0, 12, 800); x0 = 5.0
tt = np.linspace(0, 2 * T, 800)
ts = np.linspace(0, 2 * T, 40, endpoint=False)

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.9), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.4, 1]})
(wave,) = ax.plot([], [], color=TEAL, lw=2.4)
(dot,) = ax.plot([], [], "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=9, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
(lam_bar,) = ax.plot([], [], color=GRAY, lw=1.4, marker="|", ms=9)
lam_txt = ax.text(0, 1.22, r"wavelength $\lambda$: crest to crest", color=GRAY, ha="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax.axvline(x0, color=CARDINAL, lw=1, ls=":")
ax.text(x0, -1.32, r"watch the point $x_0$", color=CARDINAL, ha="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlim(0, 12); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.5); ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("u")
ax.set_title(r"snapshot in space:  $u = A\sin(kx-\omega t)$", loc="left", fontsize=11.5)

bx.plot(tt, np.sin(k * x0 - w * tt), color=GRAY, lw=1.2, alpha=0.5)
(trace,) = bx.plot([], [], color=CARDINAL, lw=2.4)
(dot2,) = bx.plot([], [], "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=9, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
bx.plot([0, T], [1.15, 1.15], color=GRAY, lw=1.4, marker="|", ms=9)
bx.text(T / 2, 1.22, "period T: crest to crest", color=GRAY, ha="center", fontsize=10.5)
bx.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
bx.set_xlim(0, 2 * T); bx.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.5); bx.set_xlabel("t"); bx.set_yticks([])
bx.set_title(r"history of the point $x_0$", loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
fig.tight_layout()

def update(i):
    t = ts[i]
    wave.set_data(x, np.sin(k * x - w * t)); dot.set_data([x0], [np.sin(k * x0 - w * t)])
    xc = ((np.pi / 2 + w * t) / k) % lam            # a crest that stays inside the window
    lam_bar.set_data([xc, xc + lam], [1.15, 1.15]); lam_txt.set_position((xc + lam / 2, 1.24))
    mask = tt <= t
    trace.set_data(tt[mask], np.sin(k * x0 - w * tt[mask])); dot2.set_data([t], [np.sin(k * x0 - w * t)])

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=100, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)

  • When describing waves it is much more convenient to work with the complex representation. One can always extract the real or imaginary part after the calculation is done.

Complex exponential representation of waves
u(x,t)=Aei(kx−ωt)u(x,t) = Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)}u(x,t)=Aei(kx−ωt)
(6)

The real part is the cosine wave and the imaginary part the sine wave. At a fixed position the exponential is a phasor, an arrow of length AAA that turns steadily in the complex plane as ttt advances.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

k, w = 2 * np.pi / 5.0, 2 * np.pi / 3.0     # lambda = 5, T = 3

(im,) = ax_w.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=2.0, ls="--", label=r"Im $e^{i(kx-\omega t)} = \sin(kx-\omega t)$")

ax_p.plot(np.cos(th), np.sin(th), color=GRAY, lw=1, ls="--")
ax_p.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6); ax_p.axvline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)

(tip,) = ax_p.plot([], [], "o", color=PURPLE, ms=8)

    re.set_data(x, np.cos(ph)); im.set_data(x, np.sin(ph))

Complex numbers refresher

The polar form reiθre^{i\theta}reiθ, Euler’s formula, and why waves are “rotating phases” are reviewed in Appendix A.2.

Periodicity in space and time¶

Sine and cosine traveling waves are periodic in space and in time. We introduce two quantities that quantify these periodicities.

  • A periodic wave repeats itself at intervals x=λx=\lambdax=λ, which is the definition of the wavelength.

  • Mathematically, one wavelength must advance the phase by one full turn: kλ=2πk\lambda=2\pikλ=2π.

Wave number kkk: periodicity in space
k=2πλk=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}k=λ2π​
(7)

  • A periodic wave repeats itself after one period t=Tt=Tt=T, or with frequency ν=1/T\nu=1/Tν=1/T (cycles per second, hertz).

  • Mathematically, one period must advance the phase by one full turn: ωT=2π\omega T=2\piωT=2π.

Angular frequency ω\omegaω: periodicity in time
ω=2πT=2πν\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi\nuω=T2π​=2πν
(8)

  • The two periodicities are not independent. In one period the wave moves forward by exactly one wavelength, so the speed is v=λ/Tv=\lambda/Tv=λ/T. The same statement in terms of kkk and ω\omegaω follows from ω=kv\omega=kvω=kv.

Speed ties space to time
v=ωk=λνv=\frac{\omega}{k}=\lambda\nuv=kω​=λν
(9)

For a wave on a string or a sound wave, vvv is a property of the medium, so fixing λ\lambdaλ fixes ν\nuν. For light in vacuum v=cv=cv=c and λν=c\lambda\nu=cλν=c. A relation between ω\omegaω and kkk is called a dispersion relation; here it is the simplest possible one, a straight line.

  • The following form makes the two periodicities explicit: the wave repeats in space at every multiple of λ\lambdaλ and in time at every multiple of TTT.

u(x,t)=Asin⁡[2π(xλ−tT)]u(x,t) = A\sin\Big[2\pi \Big(\frac{x}{\lambda} - \frac{t}{T}\Big)\Big]u(x,t)=Asin[2π(λx​−Tt​)]
(10)

Wave equation¶

  • Positions, velocities, and forces in classical mechanics are tied together by Newton’s second law, an equation with second derivatives in time. Waves obey an analogous equation of motion that ties the curvature of the shape in space to its acceleration in time. We can find it by taking derivatives of the complex wave.

Waves satisfy a wave equation

  • Take two derivatives of u=Aei(kx−ωt)u=Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)}u=Aei(kx−ωt) with respect to xxx. Each derivative brings down a factor ikikik:

∂2u∂x2=(ik)2u=−k2u\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = (ik)^2 u = -k^2u∂x2∂2u​=(ik)2u=−k2u
(11)

  • Take two derivatives with respect to ttt. Each brings down a factor −iω-i\omega−iω:

∂2u∂t2=(−iω)2u=−ω2u\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = (-i\omega)^2 u= -\omega^2u∂t2∂2u​=(−iω)2u=−ω2u
(12)

  • Divide the two results to eliminate uuu, and use ω=kv\omega = kvω=kv:

∂2u/∂x2∂2u/∂t2=k2ω2=1v2\frac{\partial^2 u/\partial x^2}{\partial^2 u/\partial t^2} = \frac{k^2}{\omega^2} = \frac{1}{v^2}∂2u/∂t2∂2u/∂x2​=ω2k2​=v21​
(13)
Any shape f(x−vt)f(x-vt)f(x−vt) satisfies the same equation

The sine wave is not special. Let u(x,t)=f(s)u(x,t)=f(s)u(x,t)=f(s) with s=x−vts=x-vts=x−vt and apply the chain rule:

∂u∂x=f′(s)∂s∂x=f′(s),∂2u∂x2=f′′(s)\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = f'(s)\frac{\partial s}{\partial x} = f'(s), \qquad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = f''(s)∂x∂u​=f′(s)∂x∂s​=f′(s),∂x2∂2u​=f′′(s)
(14)
∂u∂t=f′(s)∂s∂t=−vf′(s),∂2u∂t2=v2f′′(s)\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = f'(s)\frac{\partial s}{\partial t} = -v f'(s), \qquad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = v^2 f''(s)∂t∂u​=f′(s)∂t∂s​=−vf′(s),∂t2∂2u​=v2f′′(s)
(15)

Comparing the two second derivatives gives uxx=utt/v2u_{xx} = u_{tt}/v^2uxx​=utt​/v2 for every twice-differentiable shape fff, and the same steps with s=x+vts = x+vts=x+vt show that left-moving shapes obey it too.

Classical wave equation
∂2u(x,t)∂x2=1v2∂2u(x,t)∂t2\frac{\partial^2 u(x,t)}{\partial x^2 } = \frac{1}{v^2}\frac{\partial^2 u(x,t)}{\partial t^2}∂x2∂2u(x,t)​=v21​∂t2∂2u(x,t)​
(16)

  • This is the 1D classical wave equation. It is a partial differential equation (PDE) because uuu depends on two variables, and it is second order in both. Its solutions are functions of space and time called wave functions.

  • Both f(x−vt)f(x-vt)f(x−vt) and g(x+vt)g(x+vt)g(x+vt) solve it, and so does their sum. In fact every solution is of the form

u(x,t)=f(x−vt)+g(x+vt),u(x,t) = f(x-vt) + g(x+vt),u(x,t)=f(x−vt)+g(x+vt),
(17)

a right-moving shape plus a left-moving shape (d’Alembert’s solution). The two shapes are fixed by the initial position and initial velocity of the medium, just as a trajectory in mechanics is fixed by the initial position and velocity of a particle. The next lecture solves the wave equation on a string with fixed ends.

What the equation says physically

Read it as Newton’s second law for a string. The right side is the acceleration of one small piece of string. The left side is the curvature of the string at that piece. Where the string curves upward (a trough), the neighbors on either side sit higher and pull the piece up; where it curves downward (a crest), they pull it down; where the string is straight, the two pulls cancel and there is no acceleration. Acceleration follows curvature. The constant v2v^2v2 measures how strongly the medium responds: for a string v2=T/μv^2 = \mathcal{T}/\muv2=T/μ, tension over mass per unit length, so tighter or lighter strings carry faster waves.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"

u = 1.1 * np.exp(-x**2 / 0.9) - 0.7 * np.exp(-(x - 2.3)**2 / 0.35)      # a crest and a trough
d2 = np.gradient(np.gradient(u, x), x)                                 # curvature u_xx
xb = np.array([-2.6, -1.9, -1.35, -0.7, 0.0, 0.7, 1.35, 1.75, 2.3, 2.85, 3.4])
ub, ab = np.interp(xb, x, u), 0.32 * np.interp(xb, x, d2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))
ax.plot(x, u, color=TEAL, lw=2.8)
ax.plot(xb, ub, "o", color=TEAL, ms=7, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
for xi, ui, ai in zip(xb, ub, ab):
    if abs(ai) > 0.1:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(xi, ui + ai), xytext=(xi, ui),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=CARDINAL, lw=2.2, mutation_scale=16))
ax.text(0, 1.55, "curves down: pulled down", color=CARDINAL, ha="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax.text(2.3, -1.1, "curves up: pulled up", color=CARDINAL, ha="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax.annotate("straight here:\nno net pull", xy=(-0.7, 0.64), xytext=(-1.9, 1.15), color=GRAY, ha="center",
            fontsize=10, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=GRAY, lw=1))
ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlim(-3.2, 3.6); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.8); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_title(r"acceleration follows curvature:  $\partial^2 u/\partial t^2 = v^2\,\partial^2 u/\partial x^2$",
             loc="left", fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Fig. A snapshot of a string. Each arrow is the acceleration of a bead, proportional to the local curvature: downward on the crest, upward in the trough, zero where the string is straight.

Combining waves: interference¶

  • We are often interested in the result of several waves acting together, which is described mathematically by adding the waves.

  • Adding two solutions of the wave equation produces another solution. This is the principle of linear superposition: if uAu_AuA​ and uBu_BuB​ both solve the wave equation, so does uC=uA+uBu_C = u_A + u_BuC​=uA​+uB​. It holds because every term in the equation contains uuu to the first power.

  • Interference is the name for what superposition looks like: the combined wave can have a greater, smaller, or unchanged amplitude depending on how the crests of the two waves line up.

Wave interference: derivation

Given the two waves

Ψ1(x,t)=ei(kx−ωt+ϕ1),Ψ2(x,t)=ei(kx−ωt+ϕ2)\Psi_1(x,t) = e^{i(kx - \omega t + \phi_1)}, \qquad \Psi_2(x,t) = e^{i(kx - \omega t + \phi_2)}Ψ1​(x,t)=ei(kx−ωt+ϕ1​),Ψ2​(x,t)=ei(kx−ωt+ϕ2​)
(18)

we want their sum Ψtotal=Ψ1+Ψ2\Psi_{\text{total}} = \Psi_1 + \Psi_2Ψtotal​=Ψ1​+Ψ2​.

  1. Factor out the common exponential ei(kx−ωt)e^{i(kx - \omega t)}ei(kx−ωt):

Ψtotal(x,t)=ei(kx−ωt)(eiϕ1+eiϕ2)\Psi_{\text{total}}(x,t) = e^{i(kx - \omega t)} \left( e^{i\phi_1} + e^{i\phi_2} \right)Ψtotal​(x,t)=ei(kx−ωt)(eiϕ1​+eiϕ2​)
(19)

  1. Pull out the average phase. Write ϕ1=ϕˉ+δ/2\phi_1 = \bar\phi + \delta/2ϕ1​=ϕˉ​+δ/2 and ϕ2=ϕˉ−δ/2\phi_2 = \bar\phi - \delta/2ϕ2​=ϕˉ​−δ/2 with ϕˉ=(ϕ1+ϕ2)/2\bar\phi = (\phi_1+\phi_2)/2ϕˉ​=(ϕ1​+ϕ2​)/2 and δ=ϕ1−ϕ2\delta = \phi_1 - \phi_2δ=ϕ1​−ϕ2​:

eiϕ1+eiϕ2=eiϕˉ(eiδ/2+e−iδ/2)e^{i\phi_1} + e^{i\phi_2} = e^{i \bar\phi} \left( e^{i \delta/2} + e^{-i \delta/2} \right)eiϕ1​+eiϕ2​=eiϕˉ​(eiδ/2+e−iδ/2)
(20)

  1. Recognize a cosine. By Euler’s formula the bracket is 2cos⁡(δ/2)2\cos(\delta/2)2cos(δ/2):

eiδ/2+e−iδ/2=2cos⁡(ϕ1−ϕ22)e^{i \delta/2} + e^{-i \delta/2} = 2 \cos\left( \frac{\phi_1 - \phi_2}{2} \right)eiδ/2+e−iδ/2=2cos(2ϕ1​−ϕ2​​)
(21)

  1. Put it together:

Ψtotal(x,t)=2cos⁡(ϕ1−ϕ22)ei(kx−ωt+ϕ1+ϕ22)\Psi_{\text{total}}(x,t) = 2 \cos\left( \frac{\phi_1 - \phi_2}{2} \right) e^{i \left( kx - \omega t + \frac{\phi_1 + \phi_2}{2} \right)}Ψtotal​(x,t)=2cos(2ϕ1​−ϕ2​​)ei(kx−ωt+2ϕ1​+ϕ2​​)
(22)

Conclusion. The sum of two equal-amplitude waves is again a wave of the same kkk and ω\omegaω. Its phase is the average of the two phases and its amplitude is 2∣cos⁡(δ/2)∣2|\cos(\delta/2)|2∣cos(δ/2)∣, where δ\deltaδ is the phase difference. The amplitude is 2 (constructive) for δ=0\delta = 0δ=0 and vanishes (destructive) for δ=π\delta = \piδ=π. A phase difference of π/2\pi/2π/2 gives 2\sqrt{2}2​, in between.

  • Interference is what makes the double-slit pattern of Chapter 1. Two point sources oscillating in phase send out circular waves; along directions where the two paths differ by a whole number of wavelengths the crests arrive together and the waves reinforce, and where the paths differ by a half-integer number of wavelengths they cancel.

Source
# synced: two_source_interference
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
lam = 1.0; k, w = 2 * np.pi / lam, 2 * np.pi; d = 3 * lam
xs = np.linspace(-6, 6, 220); ys = np.linspace(0, 12, 220)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
r1, r2 = np.hypot(X + d / 2, Y), np.hypot(X - d / 2, Y)
damp = lambda r: 1 / np.sqrt(1 + r)                     # gentle 2D spreading
ts = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi / w, 30, endpoint=False)
r1f, r2f = np.hypot(xs + d / 2, 12), np.hypot(xs - d / 2, 12)
I_far = np.abs(damp(r1f) * np.exp(1j * k * r1f) + damp(r2f) * np.exp(1j * k * r2f))**2

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]})
levels = np.linspace(-1.2, 1.2, 13)
ax.set_xlim(-6, 6); ax.set_ylim(0, 12); ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.plot([-d / 2, d / 2], [0, 0], "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=8, mec="white", mew=1.2, clip_on=False, zorder=5)
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_title(r"two in-phase point sources,  $d = 3\lambda$", loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
bx.plot(xs, I_far / I_far.max(), color=CARDINAL, lw=2.4)
bx.fill_between(xs, I_far / I_far.max(), color=CARDINAL, alpha=0.12)
bx.set_xlim(-6, 6); bx.set_ylim(0, 1.1)
bx.set_xlabel("x along the far edge  (y = 12)"); bx.set_ylabel("time-averaged intensity")
bx.set_title("bright and dark fringes", loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
fig.tight_layout()
art = []

def update(i):
    t = ts[i]
    for c in art:
        c.remove()
    art.clear()
    u = damp(r1) * np.cos(k * r1 - w * t) + damp(r2) * np.cos(k * r2 - w * t)
    art.append(ax.contourf(X, Y, u, levels=levels, cmap="RdBu_r", extend="both"))

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=100, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())
Loading...

Fig. Left: two point sources (red dots) three wavelengths apart send out circular waves. The gray bands radiating outward are lines of destructive interference. Right: the time-averaged intensity along the top edge shows the bright and dark fringes of a double-slit pattern.

Move the sliders: the phase shift takes the red sum from double amplitude to zero, and the phasor panel shows why.

Standing waves from traveling waves¶

  • So far the two waves we added traveled in the same direction. Something new happens when two equal waves travel in opposite directions, which is exactly what happens on a string whose ends reflect the wave back. Using the identity sin⁡a+sin⁡b=2sin⁡a+b2cos⁡a−b2\sin a + \sin b = 2\sin\frac{a+b}{2}\cos\frac{a-b}{2}sina+sinb=2sin2a+b​cos2a−b​:

A standing wave is two counter-propagating traveling waves
sin⁡(kx−ωt)+sin⁡(kx+ωt)=2sin⁡(kx) cos⁡(ωt)\sin(kx-\omega t) + \sin(kx+\omega t) = 2\sin(kx)\,\cos(\omega t)sin(kx−ωt)+sin(kx+ωt)=2sin(kx)cos(ωt)
(23)

  • The result no longer contains the combination x∓vtx \mp vtx∓vt; space and time have separated into a product X(x) T(t)X(x)\,T(t)X(x)T(t). The shape sin⁡(kx)\sin(kx)sin(kx) stays put and only its overall height 2cos⁡(ωt)2\cos(\omega t)2cos(ωt) oscillates.

  • Points where sin⁡(kx)=0\sin(kx)=0sin(kx)=0, that is kx=nπkx = n\pikx=nπ or x=nλ/2x = n\lambda/2x=nλ/2, never move at all. They are the nodes, spaced half a wavelength apart. Halfway between them sit the antinodes, where the string swings with the full amplitude 2A2A2A.

# synced: traveling_standing
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
k, w = 1.0, 1.0                        # v = w/k = 1
x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 800)     # two wavelengths
ts = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi / w, 36, endpoint=False)
nodes = np.arange(0, 4 * np.pi + 1e-9, np.pi / k)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7.5, 5.6), sharex=True)
titles = [r"travels right:  $\sin(kx-\omega t)$", r"travels left:  $\sin(kx+\omega t)$",
          r"their sum:  $2\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$,  a standing wave"]
lines, dots = [], []
for ax, ttl, col in zip(axes, titles, [TEAL, ORANGE, CARDINAL]):
    (ln,) = ax.plot([], [], color=col, lw=2.4)
    (dt,) = ax.plot([], [], "o", color=col, ms=8, mec="white", mew=1.2)
    lines.append(ln); dots.append(dt)
    ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11.5, loc="left", pad=4); ax.set_yticks([])
axes[0].set_ylim(-1.3, 1.3); axes[1].set_ylim(-1.3, 1.3); axes[2].set_ylim(-2.5, 2.5)
axes[2].plot(x, 2 * np.sin(k * x), color=GRAY, lw=1, ls="--")
axes[2].plot(x, -2 * np.sin(k * x), color=GRAY, lw=1, ls="--")
axes[2].plot(nodes, np.zeros_like(nodes), "o", color=GRAY, ms=7, zorder=5)
axes[2].text(nodes[1], -2.2, "nodes never move", color=GRAY, fontsize=10, ha="center")
axes[2].set_xlabel("x"); axes[2].set_xlim(0, 4 * np.pi)
axes[2].set_xticks(nodes)
axes[2].set_xticklabels(["0", r"$\lambda/2$", r"$\lambda$", r"$3\lambda/2$", r"$2\lambda$"])
fig.tight_layout()

def update(i):
    t = ts[i]
    lines[0].set_data(x, np.sin(k * x - w * t))
    lines[1].set_data(x, np.sin(k * x + w * t))
    lines[2].set_data(x, 2 * np.sin(k * x) * np.cos(w * t))
    dots[0].set_data([(np.pi / 2 + w * t) / k], [1.0])                 # a crest moving right
    dots[1].set_data([(np.pi / 2 + 2 * np.pi - w * t) / k], [1.0])     # a crest moving left
    dots[2].set_data([np.pi / (2 * k)], [2 * np.cos(w * t)])           # an antinode: up and down only

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=85, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())
Loading...

Fig. Top and middle: equal waves traveling right and left; the dots ride along with a crest. Bottom: their sum is a standing wave. The gray nodes never move, the antinode (red dot) only moves up and down, and the dashed envelope ±2sin⁡(kx)\pm 2\sin(kx)±2sin(kx) is the shape the string fills out.

Example: locate the nodes

A string carries the standing wave u(x,t)=2Asin⁡(kx)cos⁡(ωt)u(x,t)=2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)u(x,t)=2Asin(kx)cos(ωt) with λ=40 cm\lambda = 40\ \text{cm}λ=40 cm. Where are the nodes and the antinodes?

Nodes sit where sin⁡(kx)=0\sin(kx)=0sin(kx)=0, i.e. kx=nπkx=n\pikx=nπ. With k=2π/λk=2\pi/\lambdak=2π/λ this gives xn=nλ/2=0, 20, 40, 60 cm,…x_n = n\lambda/2 = 0,\ 20,\ 40,\ 60\ \text{cm},\ldotsxn​=nλ/2=0, 20, 40, 60 cm,…. Antinodes sit halfway between, at x=10, 30, 50 cm,…x=10,\ 30,\ 50\ \text{cm},\ldotsx=10, 30, 50 cm,…, where ∣sin⁡(kx)∣=1|\sin(kx)|=1∣sin(kx)∣=1. Neighboring nodes are always λ/2\lambda/2λ/2 apart, so counting nodes on a vibrating string is a way of measuring its wavelength.

  • If the string is clamped at both ends, the ends must be nodes. That single requirement selects the wavelengths that fit, L=nλ/2L = n\lambda/2L=nλ/2, and leads to the discrete set of normal modes solved for in the next lecture. This is the same “waves have to fit” argument that quantized the Bohr orbits in Chapter 1.

Beats: waves of slightly different wavelength¶

  • One more superposition is worth seeing. Add two waves of equal amplitude but slightly different kkk and ω\omegaω, using cos⁡a+cos⁡b=2cos⁡a−b2cos⁡a+b2\cos a + \cos b = 2\cos\frac{a-b}{2}\cos\frac{a+b}{2}cosa+cosb=2cos2a−b​cos2a+b​:

cos⁡(k1x−ω1t)+cos⁡(k2x−ω2t)=2cos⁡ ⁣(Δk2x−Δω2t)⏟slow envelope  cos⁡ ⁣(kˉx−ωˉt)⏟fast carrier\cos(k_1x-\omega_1 t) + \cos(k_2x-\omega_2 t) = \underbrace{2\cos\!\Big(\frac{\Delta k}{2}x-\frac{\Delta\omega}{2}t\Big)}_{\text{slow envelope}} \;\underbrace{\cos\!\big(\bar k x-\bar\omega t\big)}_{\text{fast carrier}}cos(k1​x−ω1​t)+cos(k2​x−ω2​t)=slow envelope2cos(2Δk​x−2Δω​t)​​fast carriercos(kˉx−ωˉt)​​
(24)

where kˉ=(k1+k2)/2\bar k = (k_1+k_2)/2kˉ=(k1​+k2​)/2, Δk=k2−k1\Delta k = k_2-k_1Δk=k2​−k1​, and likewise for ω\omegaω.

  • The result is a fast wave at the average frequency whose amplitude is modulated by a slow envelope. The envelope repeats every 2π/Δk2\pi/\Delta k2π/Δk in space and pulses at the beat frequency Δν=∣ν2−ν1∣\Delta\nu = |\nu_2-\nu_1|Δν=∣ν2​−ν1​∣ in time. This is the wobble you hear when two guitar strings are almost, but not quite, in tune.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

v = 1.0
k1, k2 = 4.0, 5.0
w1, w2 = v * k1, v * k2
x = np.linspace(0, 20, 1600)
ts = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 40, endpoint=False)     # common period of both waves

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 4.8), sharex=True)

fig.tight_layout()

def update(i):
    t = ts[i]
    y1, y2 = np.cos(k1 * x - w1 * t), np.cos(k2 * x - w2 * t)
    l1.set_data(x, y1); l2.set_data(x, y2); ls.set_data(x, y1 + y2)

Looking ahead: wave packets

Adding two wavelengths produced one lump repeated over and over. Adding many neighboring wavelengths with suitable amplitudes cancels all the lumps but one, leaving a single localized wave packet. That is how a wave can describe a particle that is somewhere in particular, and it is why a sharply localized packet needs a wide spread of kkk: the uncertainty principle of Chapter 3 in classical clothing. Appendix A.6 works out the mathematics.

A wave you cannot surf: light and relativity¶

  • Our very first step was to ride along with the wave. A surfer moving at the wave speed vvv sees a frozen shape, and the shore observer sees that shape slide by: x=x′+vtx = x' + vtx=x′+vt. For water, sound, and strings this works because the wave lives in a medium, and “speed vvv” means speed relative to that medium.

  • Light is the exception. Maxwell’s equations of electromagnetism turn out to contain a wave equation for the electric and magnetic fields, with a speed built from two constants of nature and no medium in sight:

∂2E∂x2=1c2∂2E∂t2,c=1ε0μ0=3.00×108 m/s\frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial x^2} = \frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial t^2}, \qquad c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \mu_0}} = 3.00\times 10^8\ \text{m/s}∂x2∂2E​=c21​∂t2∂2E​,c=ε0​μ0​​1​=3.00×108 m/s
(25)

  • With no medium there is nothing for “speed relative to the medium” to mean. At sixteen, Einstein asked what a light wave would look like if he could run alongside it at ccc: a frozen electromagnetic ripple, which Maxwell’s equations do not allow. His resolution (1905) was to take the wave equation at its word: light moves at ccc for every observer, however fast that observer moves. There is no surfer frame for light, and the everyday rule x′=x−vtx' = x - vtx′=x−vt must fail at speeds near ccc.

  • The simplest consequence shows up in a light clock: a photon bouncing between two mirrors a distance ddd apart, one round trip per tick. At rest the tick lasts Δt0=2d/c\Delta t_0 = 2d/cΔt0​=2d/c. Now watch the same clock fly past at speed vvv. The photon travels a longer zigzag path, but at the same speed ccc, so each tick takes longer. Pythagoras on one half-tick, (c Δt/2)2=d2+(v Δt/2)2(c\,\Delta t/2)^2 = d^2 + (v\,\Delta t/2)^2(cΔt/2)2=d2+(vΔt/2)2, gives:

Time dilation
Δt=Δt01−v2/c2=γ Δt0,γ=11−v2/c2≥1\Delta t = \frac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = \gamma\, \Delta t_0, \qquad \gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} \geq 1Δt=1−v2/c2​Δt0​​=γΔt0​,γ=1−v2/c2​1​≥1
(26)

A moving clock ticks slower by the factor γ\gammaγ. Nothing is wrong with the clock; this is the price of ccc being the same in every inertial frame.

(mir_a1,) = ax.plot([-0.5, 0.5], [d, d], color="#333333", lw=5, solid_capstyle="butt")
(ph_a,) = ax.plot([], [], "o", color=ORANGE, ms=13, mec="#ffd27f", mew=2.5, zorder=6)
(path_a,) = ax.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=1.2, ls=":", alpha=0.8)
tick_a = ax.text(0, -0.25, "", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=TEAL, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_title(r"clock at rest:  tick $= 2d/c$", loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
ax.text(0.62, d / 2, "d", fontsize=12, color=GRAY, va="center")
ax.plot([0.58, 0.58], [0, d], color=GRAY, lw=1, marker="_", ms=8)

(mir_b0,) = bx.plot([], [], color="#333333", lw=5, solid_capstyle="butt")
(mir_b1,) = bx.plot([], [], color="#333333", lw=5, solid_capstyle="butt")
(ph_b,) = bx.plot([], [], "o", color=ORANGE, ms=13, mec="#ffd27f", mew=2.5, zorder=6)
(path_b,) = bx.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=1.2, ls=":", alpha=0.8)
tick_b = bx.text(0, -0.25, "", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=CARDINAL, fontweight="bold")
bx.annotate("", xy=(4.2, 1.32), xytext=(2.9, 1.32), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GRAY, lw=1.6))
bx.text(3.55, 1.37, "v = 0.6 c", color=GRAY, fontsize=10.5, ha="center")
bx.set_title(rf"moving at $v = 0.6c$:  longer path at the same $c$, tick $= \gamma\, 2d/c$,  $\gamma$ = {gamma:.2f}",
             loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
fig.suptitle("light moves at c for every observer, so the moving clock ticks slower", fontsize=12.5, y=0.99)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.94))

def update(i):
    t = ts[i]
    tt = np.linspace(0, t, 300)
    ph_a.set_data([0], [bounce(t / T0)])
    path_a.set_data(np.zeros_like(tt), bounce(tt / T0))
    tick_a.set_text(f"ticks: {int(t // T0)}")
    xc = v * t
    mir_b0.set_data([xc - 0.5, xc + 0.5], [0, 0]); mir_b1.set_data([xc - 0.5, xc + 0.5], [d, d])
    ph_b.set_data([xc], [bounce(t / (gamma * T0))])
    path_b.set_data(v * tt, bounce(tt / (gamma * T0)))
    tick_b.set_position((xc, -0.25)); tick_b.set_text(f"ticks: {int(t // (gamma * T0))}")

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=90, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())

Fig. Left: a light clock at rest ticks every 2d/c2d/c2d/c. Right: the same clock moving at v=0.6cv = 0.6cv=0.6c. The photon’s zigzag path is longer by γ=1.25\gamma = 1.25γ=1.25, and since ccc is unchanged the moving clock has completed fewer ticks at every instant.

Why a chemist should know this

Electrons near a heavy nucleus move fast: in the Bohr model the innermost electron of gold (Z=79Z = 79Z=79) has v/c≈Z/137≈0.58v/c \approx Z/137 \approx 0.58v/c≈Z/137≈0.58. Relativity contracts and stabilizes the 6s6s6s orbital of gold and mercury, which is why gold is yellow while silver is white, and part of why mercury is a liquid. The Schrödinger equation we build next is non-relativistic. It is excellent for light atoms and for most of chemistry, and its relativistic extension, the Dirac equation, is where electron spin comes from.

Problems¶

Problem 1: Traveling or standing¶

Which of these functions can describe a traveling wave, and with what velocity: u=(x+t)2u=(x+t)^2u=(x+t)2, u=cos⁡(x−2t)u=\cos(x-2t)u=cos(x−2t), u=cos⁡(x)sin⁡(t)u=\cos(x)\sin(t)u=cos(x)sin(t)?

Solution

If a function can be cast in the form f(x±vt)f(x\pm vt)f(x±vt), it describes a wave propagating with constant velocity vvv along the xxx axis.

  • u=(x+t)2u=(x+t)^2u=(x+t)2 has the form f(x+vt)f(x+vt)f(x+vt) with v=1v=1v=1: a wave traveling in the negative xxx direction with speed 1.

  • u=cos⁡(x−2t)u=\cos(x-2t)u=cos(x−2t) has the form f(x−vt)f(x-vt)f(x−vt) with v=2v=2v=2: a wave traveling in the positive xxx direction with speed 2.

  • u=cos⁡(x)sin⁡(t)u=\cos(x)\sin(t)u=cos(x)sin(t) cannot be written as a function of x±vtx\pm vtx±vt alone: it is a product X(x)T(t)X(x)T(t)X(x)T(t), a standing wave.

Problem 2: Wavelength and frequency¶

Given the traveling wave u(x,t)=sin⁡(2x−10t+π/2)u(x,t) = \sin(2x-10t+\pi/2)u(x,t)=sin(2x−10t+π/2) in SI units, extract its amplitude, wavelength, angular frequency, frequency, period, and velocity.

Solution

Compare with the standard form Asin⁡(kx−ωt+ϕ)A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)Asin(kx−ωt+ϕ) and read off the constants:

  • A=1A=1A=1, the multiplier in front of the sine.

  • k=2 m−1k=2\ \text{m}^{-1}k=2 m−1, hence λ=2π/k=π m≈3.14 m\lambda = 2\pi/k = \pi\ \text{m} \approx 3.14\ \text{m}λ=2π/k=π m≈3.14 m.

  • ω=10 s−1\omega = 10\ \text{s}^{-1}ω=10 s−1, the coefficient of ttt. Hence ν=ω/2π=5/π≈1.59 Hz\nu = \omega/2\pi = 5/\pi \approx 1.59\ \text{Hz}ν=ω/2π=5/π≈1.59 Hz and T=1/ν=π/5≈0.63 sT = 1/\nu = \pi/5 \approx 0.63\ \text{s}T=1/ν=π/5≈0.63 s.

  • v=ω/k=5 m/sv = \omega/k = 5\ \text{m/s}v=ω/k=5 m/s, in the positive xxx direction because the argument has the form kx−ωtkx-\omega tkx−ωt. Check: λν=π⋅5/π=5 m/s\lambda\nu = \pi \cdot 5/\pi = 5\ \text{m/s}λν=π⋅5/π=5 m/s.

  • The phase ϕ=π/2\phi = \pi/2ϕ=π/2 turns the sine into a cosine: sin⁡(θ+π/2)=cos⁡θ\sin(\theta+\pi/2) = \cos\thetasin(θ+π/2)=cosθ, so u=cos⁡(2x−10t)u = \cos(2x-10t)u=cos(2x−10t).

Problem 3: Checking the wave equation by the chain rule¶

  • A. Show by direct differentiation that the Gaussian pulse u(x,t)=e−(x−vt)2u(x,t) = e^{-(x-vt)^2}u(x,t)=e−(x−vt)2 satisfies the classical wave equation.

  • B. Does u(x,t)=x2−v2t2u(x,t) = x^2 - v^2t^2u(x,t)=x2−v2t2 satisfy it?

Solution

A. Let s=x−vts = x-vts=x−vt, so u=e−s2u = e^{-s^2}u=e−s2 and duds=−2s e−s2\dfrac{du}{ds} = -2s\,e^{-s^2}dsdu​=−2se−s2, d2uds2=(4s2−2) e−s2\dfrac{d^2u}{ds^2} = (4s^2-2)\,e^{-s^2}ds2d2u​=(4s2−2)e−s2.

By the chain rule, ∂s/∂x=1\partial s/\partial x = 1∂s/∂x=1 and ∂s/∂t=−v\partial s/\partial t = -v∂s/∂t=−v, so

∂2u∂x2=d2uds2,∂2u∂t2=(−v)2d2uds2=v2d2uds2.\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = \frac{d^2u}{ds^2}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = (-v)^2\frac{d^2u}{ds^2} = v^2\frac{d^2u}{ds^2}.∂x2∂2u​=ds2d2u​,∂t2∂2u​=(−v)2ds2d2u​=v2ds2d2u​.
(27)

Therefore ∂2u∂x2=1v2∂2u∂t2\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = \dfrac{1}{v^2}\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2}∂x2∂2u​=v21​∂t2∂2u​, as required. Nothing about the Gaussian was used: any f(x−vt)f(x-vt)f(x−vt) passes the same test.

B. Here ∂2u/∂x2=2\partial^2 u/\partial x^2 = 2∂2u/∂x2=2 while ∂2u/∂t2=−2v2\partial^2 u/\partial t^2 = -2v^2∂2u/∂t2=−2v2, so the right-hand side of the wave equation is −2≠2-2 \neq 2−2=2. It is not a solution. Note that x2−v2t2=(x−vt)(x+vt)x^2-v^2t^2 = (x-vt)(x+vt)x2−v2t2=(x−vt)(x+vt) is a product of a right-moving and a left-moving function; the wave equation only guarantees that sums f(x−vt)+g(x+vt)f(x-vt)+g(x+vt)f(x−vt)+g(x+vt) are solutions.

Problem 4: Reading a standing wave¶

A string carries the standing wave u(x,t)=0.02 sin⁡(3.14 x)cos⁡(62.8 t)u(x,t) = 0.02\,\sin(3.14\,x)\cos(62.8\,t)u(x,t)=0.02sin(3.14x)cos(62.8t) in SI units.

  • A. What are the wavelength, frequency, and speed of the two traveling waves it is made of?

  • B. How far apart are the nodes?

Solution

A. Compare with 2Asin⁡(kx)cos⁡(ωt)2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)2Asin(kx)cos(ωt): k=3.14 m−1k = 3.14\ \text{m}^{-1}k=3.14 m−1 so λ=2π/k=2.0 m\lambda = 2\pi/k = 2.0\ \text{m}λ=2π/k=2.0 m; ω=62.8 s−1\omega = 62.8\ \text{s}^{-1}ω=62.8 s−1 so ν=ω/2π=10 Hz\nu = \omega/2\pi = 10\ \text{Hz}ν=ω/2π=10 Hz. Each underlying traveling wave has amplitude A=0.01 mA = 0.01\ \text{m}A=0.01 m and speed v=ω/k=λν=20 m/sv = \omega/k = \lambda\nu = 20\ \text{m/s}v=ω/k=λν=20 m/s, one moving right and one moving left.

B. Nodes are where sin⁡(kx)=0\sin(kx) = 0sin(kx)=0, at x=nπ/k=nλ/2=0, 1, 2,… mx = n\pi/k = n\lambda/2 = 0,\ 1,\ 2,\ldots\ \text{m}x=nπ/k=nλ/2=0, 1, 2,… m. They are λ/2=1.0 m\lambda/2 = 1.0\ \text{m}λ/2=1.0 m apart.

A helium-neon laser emits light with λ=633 nm\lambda = 633\ \text{nm}λ=633 nm. Find kkk, ν\nuν, ω\omegaω, and TTT, and write the wave in complex form Aei(kx−ωt)Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)}Aei(kx−ωt) with the numerical values of kkk and ω\omegaω in SI units. How many wavelengths fit in 1 mm?

Problem 6: Tuning by beats¶

Two guitar strings sound at 440 Hz and 444 Hz.

  • A. What beat frequency does a listener hear, and what is the period of the loudness pulsation?

  • B. Sound travels at 343 m/s. What are the two wavelengths, and over what distance in space does the beat envelope repeat?
